coverage: All five chapters in both English editions: named individuals and historically identifiable titles, with literary and religious references distinguished. Unnamed legal-case examples, institutions and philosophical-school adjectives are not assigned conjectural personal identities.

entities.name: Akbar
entities.body: The Mughal emperor cited as an example of a capable absolute ruler.

entities.name: Charlemagne
entities.body: The Frankish king and emperor cited alongside Akbar.

entities.name: Auguste Comte
entities.body: The French philosopher whose system of social organization Mill criticizes.

entities.name: Socrates
entities.body: The Athenian philosopher used as a leading example in the discussion of free inquiry.

entities.name: Plato
entities.body: The Greek philosopher and pupil of Socrates.

entities.name: Aristotle
entities.body: The Greek philosopher and pupil of Plato.

entities.name: Saint Paul
entities.body: The early Christian apostle, formerly a persecutor of Christians.

entities.name: Marcus Aurelius
entities.body: The Roman emperor and Stoic thinker, also called Antoninus here.

entities.name: Constantine
entities.body: The Roman emperor associated with Christianity’s adoption by the imperial state.

entities.name: Samuel Johnson
entities.body: The English writer and critic quoted on religious persecution.

entities.name: Martin Luther
entities.body: The German religious reformer associated with the Protestant Reformation.

entities.name: Arnold of Brescia
entities.body: The medieval religious reformer cited among those suppressed before Luther.

entities.name: Fra Dolcino
entities.body: The Italian religious dissenter cited among the predecessors of the Reformation.

entities.name: Girolamo Savonarola
entities.body: The Florentine preacher and reformer cited in the discussion of persecution.

entities.name: Mary I
entities.body: The English queen whose reign is discussed in relation to Protestantism.

entities.name: Elizabeth I
entities.body: The English queen who succeeded Mary I.

entities.name: Cicero
entities.body: The Roman orator and statesman, cited for studying both sides of an argument.

entities.name: John Calvin
entities.body: The Protestant reformer whose religious teaching Mill discusses.

entities.name: John Knox
entities.body: The Scottish Protestant reformer.

entities.name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
entities.body: The philosopher whose criticism of modern civilization challenged prevailing opinion.

entities.name: Wilhelm von Humboldt
entities.body: The German scholar and statesman whose writing on individual development Mill draws on.

entities.name: Alcibiades
entities.body: The Athenian statesman and general, cited as an example of forceful individuality.

entities.name: Pericles
entities.body: The Athenian statesman whom Mill invokes as a model of developed character.

entities.name: Alexis de Tocqueville
entities.body: The French political thinker cited on growing social uniformity.

entities.name: Charles II
entities.body: The English king whose reign followed the Puritan Commonwealth.

entities.name: Lord Stanley
entities.body: Edward Henry Stanley, the British politician discussed in the correspondence on temperance restrictions.

entities.name: Jeremy Bentham
entities.body: The British philosopher and legal reformer cited on evidence.

entities.name: John Locke
entities.body: The English philosopher named as a subject for the study of philosophy.

entities.name: Immanuel Kant
entities.body: The German philosopher named alongside Locke in the education example.

entities.name: Jesus Christ
entities.body: The central figure of Christianity, whose teachings and treatment Mill discusses.

entities.name: God
entities.body: The divine being invoked in the discussion of belief, morality and religious authority.

entities.name: George Barnwell
entities.body: The young apprentice from the ballad and dramatic story used in Mill’s example about motives.

entities.name: The Czar
entities.body: The Russian emperor, used here to illustrate a ruler’s dependence on bureaucracy.
